title: Multiscale evaluation of the elastic response of polycrystalline NiAl using molecular statics, EBSD-based finite element and analytical homogenization methods
authors: Szymon Nosewicz, Marcin Maździarz, Paweł Hołobut, Witold Chromiński, Katarzyna Kowalczyk-Gajewska, Grzegorz Jurczak
abstract: The presented work proposes a multiscale framework for the numerical and analytical determination of the elastic constants of the intermetallic nickel aluminide (NiAl) at the microscopic scale. Molecular dynamics (MD) calculations have been employed to evaluate the stiffness tensors of a single NiAl monocrystalline body with cubic Pm$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The atomistic results were transferred to the upper scale as an input to micromechanical models. Here, finite element modeling (FEM) and analytical homogenization methods were used to simulate the elastic behavior of polycrystalline NiAl, with special attention to grain anisotropy and its morphology. The microstructural features of the heterogeneous body were evaluated experimentally using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and subsequently used to generate a 3D polycrystalline geometric model that preserves realistic distributions of grain orientations and grain sizes. The reconstructed NiAl polycrystal was subjected to uniaxial tensile test simulations using FEM to evaluate the effective Young's modulus ($E$) and Poisson's ratio ($ν$). The numerical results were confronted with the experimental values of $E$ and~$ν$. With these model assumptions, a very good agreement between numerical and experimental results was achieved. Finally, the experimental results were compared with classical analytical estimates. Among the analytical approaches, the Hashin-Shtrikman upper bound and self-consistent approximation reproduced the experimental Young's modulus with minor deviations.
summary: This work establishes a multiscale computational framework to predict the elastic properties of polycrystalline NiAl. It integrates atomistic simulations (MD) to find single-crystal stiffness, uses EBSD data to build realistic microstructures, and then employs FEM to simulate the bulk response. The successful comparison between numerical predictions and experimental data validates the comprehensive multiscale approach.
main_problem: The paper aims to determine the elastic constants and effective elastic response of polycrystalline NiAl by developing a multiscale framework that integrates atomistic simulations with continuum mechanics.
main_result: The multiscale approach achieved very good agreement between the numerically simulated effective Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio, and the experimentally measured values.
method: The methodology combines Molecular Dynamics (MD) for single-crystal stiffness tensors, Finite Element Modeling (FEM) using EBSD-generated 3D microstructures, and analytical homogenization techniques.
model_or_system: The physical system is intermetallic nickel aluminide (NiAl) in a polycrystalline state. The model incorporates realistic microstructural features, grain orientations, and grain sizes derived from Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) data.
key_observables: Effective Young’s modulus (E) and Poisson’s ratio (ν); stiffness tensors (C); elastic constants.
important_parameters: Grain anisotropy and morphology; single-crystal stiffness tensors derived from MD calculations.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the elastic behavior can be accurately modeled by combining atomistically derived properties with continuum approximations, though classical analytical methods are noted to rely on strong assumptions.
figures_summary: The notes mention figures illustrating atomistic models for different lattice vector orientations and an overview of the EBSD-based reconstruction workflow used for the FEM simulations.
paper_structure: The paper follows a multiscale progression: first, determining single-crystal properties via MD; second, reconstructing the complex polycrystal geometry using EBSD data; third, simulating the bulk response using FEM; and finally, comparing these results against analytical bounds and experimental measurements.
why_interesting: While focused on materials science, the core methodology—combining atomistic simulations (MD) with continuum modeling (FEM) across multiple length scales—is a general computational framework relevant to many-body dynamics simulations in condensed matter theory.
